[2020 summer phd probability — problem 2]

A population in which each individual is at any time in one of three states $A$, $B$, $C$ evolves in discrete time: (1) each individual in state $A$ in generation $n$ produces a random number $\xi_x$ of offspring in generation $n+1$, all of type $B$, then dies, where $P(\xi_x = k) = \alpha^k(1-\alpha)$, $k = 0,1,2,\dots$, for $0 < \alpha < 1$; (2) each individual in state $B$ in generation $n$ mutates to state $A$ with probability $p$ or to state $C$ with probability $q = 1-p$ ($0 < p < 1$); (3) each individual in state $C$ dies; (4) all individuals act independently. Let $Z^i_n$ be the number of individuals in state $i$ in generation $n$; assume $Z^A_0 = 1$ (a single individual in state $A$ at time $0$).
(a) Show that with probability $1$, either $Z^A_n = Z^B_n = Z^C_n = 0$ for all large $n$, or $\lim_{n\to\infty}(Z^A_n + Z^B_n + Z^C_n) = \infty$.
(b) Express $\mathbb{E}(Z^A_n)$, $\mathbb{E}(Z^B_n)$ and $\mathbb{E}(Z^C_n)$ as functions of $\alpha$, $p$ and $n$.
(c) Let $p_e = P(Z^A_n = Z^B_n = Z^C_n = 0 \text{ for all large } n)$ be the extinction probability. For which values of $\alpha$ and $p$ is $p_e = 1$? Give a proof.
(d) In the case $p_e < 1$, find an explicit closed-form expression for $p_e$ in terms of $\alpha$ and $p$.
(e) Define sequences $\{a(n)\}_{n\ge1}$ and $\{b(n)\}_{n\ge1}$ such that $Y_n := Z^B_{a(n)}/b(n)$ converges almost surely to a finite limiting random variable. Give explicit forms of $a(n), b(n)$ and prove the convergence.

response.text:
Let

\[
\mu:=E\xi=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha},\qquad q=1-p,\qquad 
\rho:=\mu p=\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}.
\]

The key observation is that, starting from one \(A\)-individual at time \(0\), the \(A\)-population can appear only at even times, the \(B\)-population only at odd times, and \(C\)-individuals only at even times. Define

\[
W_k:=Z^A_{2k},\qquad k\ge 0.
\]

An \(A\)-individual at time \(2k\) produces \(\xi\) many \(B\)-children at time \(2k+1\), and each of those becomes an \(A\) at time \(2k+2\) with probability \(p\). Hence the number of \(A\)-grandchildren of one \(A\)-individual has distribution

\[
\eta=\sum_{j=1}^{\xi} I_j,
\]

where \(I_j\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\) independently. Therefore \(\{W_k\}_{k\ge0}\) is a one-type Galton–Watson process with offspring generating function

\[
\phi(s)=E[s^\eta]
=E[(q+ps)^\xi]
=\sum_{m=0}^\infty (1-\alpha)\alpha^m(q+ps)^m
=\frac{1-\alpha}{1-\alpha(q+ps)}.
\]

Also

\[
\phi'(1)=E\eta=\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}=\rho.
\]

---

## (a) Extinction or explosion

The full process becomes extinct eventually iff the Galton–Watson process \(W_k=Z^A_{2k}\) becomes extinct.

Indeed, if \(W_k=0\), then there are no \(A\)-individuals at time \(2k\). There may be \(C\)-individuals at time \(2k\), but they die and produce no descendants, so the whole population is zero from time \(2k+1\) onward. Conversely, if the whole population dies out, then certainly \(W_k=0\) eventually.

Now \(W_k\) is an ordinary Galton–Watson process. Since

\[
P(\eta=0)=\phi(0)=\frac{1-\alpha}{1-\alpha q}>0,
\]

a standard Galton–Watson dichotomy applies: on the survival event,

\[
W_k\to\infty \qquad \text{a.s.}
\]

For completeness, here is the argument. Fix \(N\ge1\). Whenever \(1\le W_k\le N\),

\[
P(W_{k+1}=0\mid W_k)\ge P(\eta=0)^N>0.
\]

Thus, by the strong Markov property, on the event of nonextinction the process can visit \(\{1,\dots,N\}\) only finitely often. Since this holds for every \(N\), on nonextinction we must have \(W_k\to\infty\).

On that event,

\[
Z^A_{2k}=W_k\to\infty.
\]

Also,

\[
Z^A_{2k+2}\le Z^B_{2k+1},
\]

because each \(A\)-individual at time \(2k+2\) comes from a distinct \(B\)-individual at time \(2k+1\). Therefore

\[
Z^B_{2k+1}\to\infty.
\]

Hence along both parity subsequences the total population goes to infinity. Therefore, with probability \(1\), either the population is eventually extinct or

\[
Z^A_n+Z^B_n+Z^C_n\to\infty.
\]

---

## (b) Expectations

The mean recursions are

\[
E[Z^A_{n+1}]=p\,E[Z^B_n],
\]

\[
E[Z^B_{n+1}]=\mu\,E[Z^A_n],
\]

\[
E[Z^C_{n+1}]=q\,E[Z^B_n].
\]

With \(Z^A_0=1\) and \(Z^B_0=Z^C_0=0\), we get the parity structure

\[
E[Z^A_{2k+1}]=0,\qquad E[Z^B_{2k}]=0,\qquad E[Z^C_{2k+1}]=0.
\]

For even \(A\)-generations,

\[
E[Z^A_{2k}]=\rho^k.
\]

For odd \(B\)-generations,

\[
E[Z^B_{2k+1}]
=\mu\,E[Z^A_{2k}]
=\mu\rho^k.
\]

For \(C\)-individuals, for \(k\ge1\),

\[
E[Z^C_{2k}]
=q\,E[Z^B_{2k-1}]
=q\mu\rho^{k-1}.
\]

Thus explicitly,

\[
\boxed{
E[Z^A_{2k}]=\rho^k,\qquad E[Z^A_{2k+1}]=0
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
E[Z^B_{2k}]=0,\qquad E[Z^B_{2k+1}]=\mu\rho^k
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
E[Z^C_0]=0,\qquad E[Z^C_{2k}]=q\mu\rho^{k-1}\ \text{for }k\ge1,\qquad E[Z^C_{2k+1}]=0.
}
\]

Equivalently, substituting \(\mu=\alpha/(1-\alpha)\),

\[
\rho=\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}.
\]

---

## (c) Values of \(\alpha,p\) for which \(p_e=1\)

The extinction probability of the full process equals the extinction probability of the Galton–Watson process \(W_k\). For a Galton–Watson process, extinction occurs a.s. iff the offspring mean is at most \(1\). Here the mean is

\[
\rho=\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}.
\]

Therefore

\[
p_e=1
\iff \rho\le1
\iff \frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}\le1
\iff \alpha p\le 1-\alpha
\iff \alpha(1+p)\le1.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
p_e=1 \iff \alpha\le \frac1{1+p}.
}
\]

Equivalently, survival has positive probability iff

\[
\boxed{
\alpha>\frac1{1+p}.
}
\]

---

## (d) Closed form for \(p_e\) when \(p_e<1\)

The extinction probability is the smallest solution \(s\in[0,1]\) of

\[
s=\phi(s)=\frac{1-\alpha}{1-\alpha(q+ps)}.
\]

Thus

\[
s\bigl(1-\alpha q-\alpha ps\bigr)=1-\alpha,
\]

so

\[
\alpha p s^2-(1-\alpha q)s+(1-\alpha)=0.
\]

Since \(q=1-p\), this quadratic factors as

\[
\alpha p(s-1)\left(s-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha p}\right)=0.
\]

The two roots are

\[
s=1,\qquad s=\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha p}=\frac1\rho.
\]

In the supercritical case \(p_e<1\), we have \(\rho>1\), so \((1-\alpha)/(\alpha p)<1\). Therefore the extinction probability is the smaller root:

\[
\boxed{
p_e=\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha p}.
}
\]

This applies precisely when

\[
\boxed{
\alpha>\frac1{1+p}.
}
\]

---

## (e) Almost sure normalization for \(Z^B_n\)

A natural choice is to look only at odd times, since \(Z^B_{2k}=0\). Define, for \(n\ge1\),

\[
\boxed{
a(n)=2n-1,
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
b(n)=\mu \rho^{\,n-1}
=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}
\left(\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}\right)^{n-1}.
}
\]

Then

\[
Y_n:=\frac{Z^B_{2n-1}}{\mu\rho^{n-1}}.
\]

Assume first that \(\rho>1\). Let

\[
M_k:=\frac{W_k}{\rho^k}
=\frac{Z^A_{2k}}{\rho^k}.
\]

Since \(W_k\) is a Galton–Watson process with mean offspring number \(\rho\), \(\{M_k\}\) is a nonnegative martingale. By the martingale convergence theorem,

\[
M_k\to M_\infty
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

for some finite random variable \(M_\infty\).

Now condition on the population at time \(2k\). Given \(W_k\), the number of \(B\)-children at time \(2k+1\) is

\[
Z^B_{2k+1}=\sum_{j=1}^{W_k}\xi_{k,j},
\]

where the \(\xi_{k,j}\) are i.i.d. copies of \(\xi\), with

\[
E\xi=\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\xi)=\frac{\alpha}{(1-\alpha)^2}<\infty.
\]

Define

\[
R_k:=\frac{Z^B_{2k+1}-\mu W_k}{\rho^k}.
\]

Then

\[
E[R_k\mid W_k]=0,
\]

and

\[
E[R_k^2]
=
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\xi)\,E[W_k]}{\rho^{2k}}
=
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\xi)\rho^k}{\rho^{2k}}
=
\operatorname{Var}(\xi)\rho^{-k}.
\]

Since \(\rho>1\),

\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty E[R_k^2]<\infty.
\]

By Chebyshev’s inequality and the Borel–Cantelli lemma,

\[
R_k\to0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Therefore

\[
\frac{Z^B_{2k+1}}{\mu\rho^k}
=
\frac{W_k}{\rho^k}
+
\frac{R_k}{\mu}
\to M_\infty
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Replacing \(k\) by \(n-1\), we obtain

\[
\boxed{
\frac{Z^B_{2n-1}}{\mu\rho^{n-1}}
\to M_\infty
\qquad\text{a.s.}
}
\]

Thus \(Y_n\) converges almost surely to the finite limiting random variable \(M_\infty\).

If \(\rho\le1\), then by part (c) extinction occurs a.s., so \(Z^B_{2n-1}=0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Hence with the same choice of \(a(n)\) and \(b(n)\), we have

\[
Y_n\to0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

So the above normalization works in all regimes, and in the supercritical case it gives the usual nontrivial Galton–Watson martingale limit.
